Assert

uh-SURT — rhymes with 'dessert'; someone who asserts serves up their opinion with confidence. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To assert to state a fact forcefully and with confidence.

The scientist continued to assert that the results were accurate, even as critics raised objections.

Worked Example

A new employee is blamed for a mistake she didn't make. Instead of staying quiet, she calmly but firmly tells her manager, in front of the whole team, exactly what really happened and why she isn't at fault.

Speaking up firmly and confidently to state the truth is to assert something. Unlike 'mention,' which is casual, to assert means to state a claim with real conviction.

How Assert Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

declare

declare: to state something officially or clearly

insist

insist: to demand or state firmly, refusing to back down

affirm

affirm: to state something as true, often confidently

Antonyms

deny

deny: to state that something is not true

doubt

doubt: to feel uncertain about the truth of something

How Strong Is It? — mention → assert → demand

mention vs. assert

mention vs. assert: Mention is weaker than assert — mentioning something is casual, while asserting means stating it forcefully and standing behind it.

demand vs. assert

demand vs. assert: Demand is stronger than assert: asserting is stating something with confidence, but demanding requires an immediate response or action from someone else.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — as- (ad-)

prefix — as- (ad-): to (Latin)

root — -sert-

root — -sert-: to join, to put in order (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Latin asserere combined ad- (to) with serere (to join, to arrange in a row). To assert something is to firmly put a claim forward, joining your words to a stated position.

Use the root in a new word: insert
